note: The original is a re-treatment in an appendix: the holotype alate is fragmentary, with the compound eyes collapsed and the colour long faded, and the worker caste is missing, so no separate measurement table is given and only a comparison with A. chirotus is made; this entry contains no measurement values.

sections.label: Diagnostic characters
sections.text: The alate agrees with Acholotermes chirotus in most measurements and compound ratios and falls to that species in the key; it differs in the slightly longer postclypeus, the narrower and more elongate oval fontanelle, and the larger ocelli. Because the holotype is fragmentary, with the compound eyes collapsed, and the specimen is severely faded from long preservation, comparison is difficult; on this basis the author does not place A. chirotus as a synonym of this species, and considers that material from intermediate localities may in future show the two to be conspecific.

sections.label: Other
sections.text: Originally Eutermes socialis Sjöstedt, 1899. Silvestri (1914) transferred it to Anoplotermes on the basis of non-type series material, Sjöstedt (1926) then placed it in Pericapritermes, and the combination remained in general use in West Africa thereafter. Sands (1972), examining the lectotype labelled by Emerson in 1952 within the type series, placed it in the new genus Acholotermes and formally published the lectotype designation: alate, Mungo River, Cameroon, 1874, ninth month (September), collected by R. Bucholz, deposited in Naturhistoriska Riksmuseum, Stockholm. Material previously recorded as Pericapritermes socialis was recognised as misidentified, and a separate species, Pericapritermes nigerianus, was established (a variety of Silvestri raised to species rank).
